summary: Specifies a form of response to a one-time password challenge that states how the response is encoded. It also defines a response that lets a generator ask the server to re-initialize a sequence and change parameters like the secret pass phrase.

plainLanguage.summary: One-time passwords are used once and thrown away. This adds a way to say how a password is written, and to start a fresh batch when you run low.

questions: how to reinitialize a one-time password sequence
what is an otp extended response
how to re-initialize a one-time password sequence

subtitle: A way for a one-time-password response to say how it is encoded, and to restart a password sequence.

tldr.problem: A plain one-time password response can occasionally be valid as both a hexadecimal number and a six-word phrase, and the original OTP system gave clients no standard way to re-initialize their sequence with a server.
tldr.mechanism: Extended responses are colon-separated lines that start with a type label such as hex, word, init-hex or init-word, so the encoding is stated outright and a re-initialization can carry new parameters and a new password.
tldr.outcome: Servers that support extended responses must handle all four types, and generators may only use them after the server advertises support in an extended challenge.

today: RFC 2243 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1997. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Extended Challenges and Responses
sections.content:
This document builds on the one-time password system (OTP) of RFC 1938 and assumes you have read it. An extended challenge is a single line holding a standard OTP challenge, a whitespace character, and a capability list that begins with ext and may name extension sets, for example otp-md5 123 mi1234 ext,foo.

An extended response is a single line of printable text made of two or more tokens separated by single colons. The first token is a type specifier that says how to read the rest, and at least one token of data MUST follow. The RFC gives the grammar in three ways: a manual-page style syntax, augmented BNF and examples. If they conflict, the BNF wins.
sections.plainLanguage: A challenge is the server asking, 'Prove it is you.' An extended response is an answer with a label on the front, like writing 'this is a number' or 'this is a list of words' before the answer.

sections.title: Rules for Servers and Generators
sections.content:
A compliant server MUST be able to parse the general form of an extended response and process every type defined in this document. It MUST treat the type field case-insensitively, MUST reject a response whose type it does not support, and SHOULD tell the generator when that is the reason. It MUST limit input length reasonably, accept arbitrary whitespace where the response allows it, and still handle standard OTP responses.

A compliant generator (the software that produces the response) MUST be able to produce standard responses and MUST use them unless it has received an extended challenge for that server and seed. It MUST write the type field in lower case and MUST NOT send a type the server has not advertised.

Extension identifiers beginning with x- are reserved for private use among consenting implementations, and an implementation that does not recognise one MUST ignore it. The rest of the namespace is reserved to IANA, which assigns names only after the IESG approves.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides follow manners. The server only accepts labels it knows. The sender only uses a label if the server said it understands it, and writes the label in small letters.

sections.title: The hex and word Responses
sections.content:
In a very rare case a standard OTP response is valid in both hexadecimal and six-word formats. The RFC's example is ABE ACE ADA ADD BAD A. The OTP specification handles this by requiring servers to try both formats and accept if either verifies.

Extended responses remove the ambiguity. A hex response is hex: followed by a 64-bit hexadecimal number, and a word response is word: followed by six dictionary words. Examples are hex:8720 33d4 6202 9172 and word:VAST SAUL TAKE SODA SUCH BOLT.

Servers MUST process all arguments case-insensitively. Generators SHOULD write words in upper case separated by single spaces, and hexadecimal letters in lower case.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a secret could be read two ways, like a word that is also a number. Putting 'hex' or 'word' in front tells the reader which way to read it.

sections.title: Re-initializing a Sequence
sections.content:
The OTP specification requires a way for a client to re-initialize its OTP information but does not define a protocol. Implementations of extended responses MUST support init-hex and init-word, which are meant mainly for automated clients, so hexadecimal is the recommended form.

The shape is init-hex:<current-OTP>:<new-params>:<new-OTP>. The current OTP answers the server's present challenge. The new parameters are an algorithm (md4, md5 or sha1), a sequence number and a seed, separated by spaces. The new OTP answers the new challenge those parameters describe. In init-hex every appropriate field MUST be hexadecimal, and in init-word every one MUST be six-word coded. Responses MUST NOT span more than one line in actual use.

If re-initialization succeeds, the server MUST store the new OTP as the last successful one, and the next challenge's sequence number MUST be one less than the number in the new parameters. The new-params field is hashed as a string, like a seed or secret pass phrase, while other fields are hashed in uncoded binary form in network byte order with no padding.
sections.plainLanguage: When you are nearly out of secret words, you prove who you are with your current word, say how the new batch works, and hand over the first new word, all in one message.

sections.title: Re-initialization Safeguards
sections.content:
Servers SHOULD NOT let a user pick the same value for seed and secret pass phrase. They MUST disable all OTP access for any principal whose sequence number would drop below one. If a re-initialization carries a valid current OTP but the server cannot process the new parameters or new OTP, the server MUST still decrement the sequence number.

Generators SHOULD also avoid identical seed and pass phrase, MUST take steps to prevent infinite loops of failed re-initialization attempts, and SHOULD show the user that re-initialization is happening. They SHOULD NOT re-initialize, or retry a failed attempt, without the user's permission. They SHOULD warn when the sequence number falls below ten and MUST refuse to generate OTPs with a sequence number below one.
sections.plainLanguage: There are safety rules so nobody gets stuck in a loop or runs out of words by surprise: ask the user first, warn when the supply is low, and stop when it hits zero.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security considerations of the OTP system also apply here. Extended responses, like OTP itself, do not protect against active attacks, so the IPsec Authentication Header (or a technique at least as strong) SHOULD be used.

An active attack on the re-initialization response can be worse than hijacking one session. An attacker who substitutes their own response for the legitimate user's may be able to authenticate as that user at will, until detected. Skipping the server requirement to decrement the sequence number after a failed re-initialization opens the server to replay of the current-OTP part of the response.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster can sit in the middle, a restart message is the juiciest thing to tamper with, because they could take over your secret-word list. Extra protection on the connection helps stop that.
